source.title: Coupled Scaling: A Representational Accessibility Framework for Neural Scaling Laws

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops a formal refinement in which acquisition patterns and task–system pairing can produce different residual-loss rates, and it reports constructed examples with differing rates. It does not directly reproduce language-model pretraining scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper’s orthogonal and fixed-kernel results are theoretical specializations, not measurements of held-out language-model cross-entropy. Its audit of released benchmark trajectories measures task-ordering summaries, not loss scaling, so those results are recorded as findings that fit none of the listed versions. Outcomes cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper. Its scaling results are derivations in an orthogonal support-and-acquisition model and a fixed-kernel gradient-flow model, plus numerical evaluations of constructed acquisition orders (Fig. 1). None measures held-out loss of language models or any trained neural system across parameters, tokens or compute. V7 concerns fitted exponents of published (language-model) laws depending on setup and fitting choices. The paper's results show rate dependence only inside an abstract model, which is a different kind of system. The released-trajectory audit (Pythia, Amber, OLMo2) measures task-ordering agreement across checkpoints, not loss scaling or downstream predictability. The paper motivates and discusses scaling laws but its own results bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that support and acquisition jointly determine task-conditioned residual loss. The completed prefix bounds the rate within a sharp interval, and the product rate applies under the rank-window condition. Common-tail comparisons turn cross-task acquisition reversals into exponent reversals. They also conclude that the released-trajectory audit is descriptive and cannot identify the mechanism. They propose a staged test: first verify the exact bound in a small system with observable ranks, then test held-out geometry-to-scaling prediction in feature-learning networks.
record.recipe_differences: A theoretical orthogonal acquisition model and fixed-kernel specialization, plus a reanalysis of released benchmark trajectories; not a language-model pretraining scaling sweep or compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The constructed residual exponent changes with acquisition order and prefix-growth conditions. In the released-data audit, max-slope and AUC summaries yield different matched contrasts; the AUC integration axis and task universe are also varied.

fits_no_version.finding: In an orthogonal support-and-acquisition model with target powers a_j≍j^-b and completed-prefix growth N^ρ, attainable residual exponents span [ρ(b−1), min{b−1, ρb}]. Every rate in that interval is realised by some fixed order on a common support. Constructed curves with b=1.6 give slopes .149, .254, .397 and .605.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In idealised acquisition models, the scaling exponent is not fixed by the target tail and prefix growth alone; acquisition order beyond the first gap can change it.

fits_no_version.finding: The product law α=ρ(b−1) holds under a bounded-gain or unresolved-rank-window condition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the orthogonal model, completed-prefix growth determines the residual exponent only under an additional acquisition condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Released-trajectory audit: within-composite matched max-slope contrast is −0.068 (primary) and −0.103 (registry). The AUC contrast is +0.029 and +0.084, and both AUC ranges span zero. AUC direction holds under an integration-axis change (+0.061, +0.121).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent implicit-curriculum ordering in released checkpoint trajectories depends on the summary measure and on how tasks are matched.

record.problems: The empirical audit uses four runs from three model families, with model family, size, recipe, checkpoint structure, evaluation, and randomness varying jointly. The authors describe the matched audit as observational and state that it cannot identify the accessibility mechanism. Some resampling intervals have undetermined conservativeness; permutation-reference areas are descriptive rather than calibrated significance probabilities. The formal scaling results concern specified mathematical models, not language-model cross-entropy.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. The audit’s other task-ordering tables and cited studies are not entered as separate rows because they do not test the listed scaling versions or are reported as external results.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other-modality, repeated-data or transfer scaling measurement.
The audit measures task-emergence ordering agreement, not downstream performance as a function of scale or loss.

No refitting of published laws and no test of sensitivity to parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method on real models. Rate dependence on acquisition order is shown only in an abstract model.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with V7 'supports' is not adopted. V7 is about fitted exponents of real (language-model) scaling laws varying with setup and fitting choices. This paper's rate variation is proved inside a constructed mathematical model with no trained network. A row bears on a version only if it concerns the same kind of system, so R1–R6 are relinked to none. Empirical exponent-dependence results mentioned in the paper (Ngo & Ravanbakhsh, Ramani & Jain, Jha & Reagen, Wang et al.) are cited from other studies and are correctly not rows. The paper is a preprint with LLM-assistance disclosure.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep on language models over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of much larger language-model runs from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or comparison of parameter- and token-growth exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The audit measures task-emergence ordering across checkpoints, not whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.

The formal results show rate dependence on acquisition structure in a specified model, but do not test published language-model exponent disagreement, parameter-counting or fitting-method sensitivity, compute-optimal allocations, or empirical departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: orthogonal support-and-acquisition model
rows.operation_detail: Derives residual-loss rates for power-law target energies under different acquisition orders.
rows.value: Attainable exponent interval [ρ(b − 1), min{b − 1, ρb}]; every rate in the interval is attained by a fixed acquisition order on a common support.
rows.note: Formal result in the paper’s model: rates vary with acquisition order even when target-power tail and completed-prefix growth are specified.
rows.check: Formal interval for residual-loss exponents in an abstract orthogonal model. It is not a fitted exponent of a language model or other trained system, so it does not measure what V7 names.
